pulls.title: zmq: Log bind error at Error level, abort startup on init error
pulls.body:
## History

This picks up #33727, which was closed for inactivity

## Problem

Currently when a user configures -zmqpub* and the socket can't be bound, the program proceeds normally. The only trace is a debug-level log line that's invisible in a default configuration.

#33715 hit this when their port was already taken.

## What this PR does
The node refuses to start if ZMQ is configured and setup failed. This failure is now logged at error level. 

Code path: 
GetNotifiers builds the notifier objects from the config; Create initializes them — starts the ZMQ engine and binds each socket. When initialization fails, Initialize() returns a util::Result carrying an error that names the notifier, the address and the OS error. Create() propagates it and init.cpp returns InitError with that message. On a node with no -zmqpub* option, the notifier list is empty.

## Why abort?
#17445 fixed bitcoind crash from bad assert due to ZMQ config (issue #17185). 
Issue #33715 reports that when ZMQ port was already taken, bitcoind started but user could not see anything with getzmqnotifications. Maintainers at the time agreed it should log louder and abort at startup. Which is what this PR fixes. 

## Testing

bitcoind -regtest -zmqpubhashblock=foo
Result: exits with code 1, and prints:

```
[error] Failed to bind address foo for pubhashblock: Invalid argument
Error: Failed to bind address foo for pubhashblock: Invalid argument
```

interface_zmq.py asserts the exact full error message for five startup-failure cases: invalid address, invalid address on a later notifier after an earlier one bound successfully (partial success must still abort), unreachable IP (EADDRNOTAVAIL), and a port already taken by the node's own RPC server (EADDRINUSE, via rpc_port()). The expected errno text is derived with os.strerror on the platform running the test, since the string after the last ":" differs per platform; on Windows the two strings libzmq hardcodes are pinned instead.

Verified locally on Windows; the full CI matrix is green on my fork.

A node with no -zmqpub* options starts exactly as before — nothing changes for nodes that don't use ZMQ.

pulls.title: kernel: allow only one global logging connection
pulls.body:
Kernel logging is inherently global: `KernelLogger` is a process-wide
singleton, so every connection receives every log entry and shares the
minimum level. Multiple `btck_LoggingConnection` handles give the false
impression of independent loggers.

Limit `btck_global_logging_connection_create` to a single connection, so
that the globalness is expressed in that one function and the rest of
the interface can operate on the connection handle.

A single connection also makes it straightforward to invoke the callback
without holding the logger's mutex. Holding it serializes all logging
threads on user code, and deadlocks if anything on the callback's thread
logs, e.g. a garbage collector running finalizers that destroy kernel
objects.

Behaviour changes for consumers:
- `btck_logging_connection_create` is renamed to
  `btck_global_logging_connection_create`, and fails if a connection
  already exists.
- `btck_logging_set_min_level` becomes
  `btck_logging_connection_set_min_level`, and each new connection
  starts at `Info`.
- The "Logger connected." `Debug` entry is removed, since it can no
  longer be delivered.
- The callback can be invoked from multiple threads at the same time,
  so it must be thread-safe. Destroying the connection still waits for
  running invocations to return.

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: tracing: run USDT tests without BPF privileges
pulls.body:
The USDT functional tests currently use BCC to attach eBPF programs to Bitcoin Core’s tracepoints. This requires BCC, matching kernel headers, and elevated BPF permissions, making the tests awkward to run locally and
requiring a privileged container in CI.

Replace the BCC consumers with GDB. Each tested node runs as a debugger child, allowing the tests to enable the real USDT probes and inspect their arguments when execution reaches the probe location. This continues to test
the parts of the USDT interface provided by Bitcoin Core:

- the probe metadata is present and understood;
- the probes can be enabled and are reached in the expected scenarios; and
- their arguments have the expected values, sizes, and lifetimes.

All five tests can run with GDB and `binutils`, without BCC or matching kernel headers. The ASan CI job no longer needs a privileged container and uses `SYS_PTRACE` instead. This also removes the embedded BPF programs from
the tests, reducing their size and maintenance burden. Overall, the change removes roughly 660 lines of test and CI code.

#### Tradeoffs

- These tests no longer exercise the consumer-side eBPF path, including BCC   compilation, kernel BPF verification and loading, uprobe attachment, BPF-side argument decoding, and perf-buffer delivery. Problems confined to
  those components would no longer be detected here.
- LeakSanitizer is disabled for nodes run under GDB because it cannot operate under `ptrace`. Other sanitizer checks remain enabled.

The remaining coverage is focused on Bitcoin Core’s side of the USDT interface. Testing the general BCC, eBPF, and kernel uprobe is left to those consumers and the kernel.

pulls.title: contrib: Skip llvm-cov rendering for deterministic fuzz inputs
pulls.body:
## Summary                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                              
  `deterministic-fuzz-coverage` rendered a full `llvm-cov show` report for every                                                                              
  fuzz input on both runs and diffed the two reports, even though almost all                                                                                  
  inputs are deterministic. `llvm-cov show` is by far the most expensive step, so                                                                             
  the vast majority of that work produced two identical reports that were                                                                                     
  immediately discarded.                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                              
  Compare the merged `.profdata` first: identical counters are a sufficient                                                                                   
  condition for deterministic coverage, so when the two profdata files match the                                                                              
  `llvm-cov show` rendering is skipped entirely. Only when they differ does it                                                                                
  fall back to rendering and diffing the reports to confirm and locate the                                                                                    
  difference.                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                              
  The pass/fail result is unchanged: identical profdata implies identical                                                                                     
  counters, which implies identical `llvm-cov show` output (the report is a                                                                                   
  deterministic function of the profdata and the binary). Any profdata difference                                                                             
  falls back to the exact same `llvm-cov` diff as before.                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                              
  ## Benchmark                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                              
  standalone coverage build (`-DBUILD_FOR_FUZZING=ON` +                                                                                                       
  `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping`, no sanitizer), par=4,                                                                                        
  qa-assets corpora:                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                              
  | target            | inputs | before | after | speedup |                                                                                                   
  |-------------------|-------:|-------:|------:|--------:|                                                                                                   
  | addition_overflow |    112 |    32s |   10s |    3.2x |                                                                                                   
  | process_message   |   2386 |   719s |  247s |    2.9x |                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                                                              
  On `process_message` every input is deterministic, so all 2386 take the                                                                                     
  profdata fast path and zero `llvm-cov show` reports are rendered, down from                                                                                 
  2*2386 + 2 = 4774.

pulls.title: logging: rewrite macros to enforce restrictions at compile-time, improve efficiency and usability
pulls.body:
This PR is an internal cleanup for `util/log.h` that fixes several problems with the logging macros defined there.

The main change is replacing the internal `detail_LogWithSrcLoc` macro with a `LOG_EMIT` macro. It makes all the external logging macros (`LogDebug`, `LogInfo`, etc.) call `LOG_EMIT`, eliminating inconsistencies, improving efficiency, and producing clearer compiler errors when called incorrectly.

Specific problems this PR fixes:

- Current logging macros duplicate logic and have undocumented, untested differences. For example, some macros evaluate their arguments when logging is disabled and others do not. By constrast, the `LOG_EMIT` macro implements logging logic in one place, preventing hidden inconsistencies.

- Current logging macros produce hard to decipher syntax errors when category arguments are specified but not allowed, or required but not provided. Now all logging macros produce clear `static_assert` errors indicating whether to add or remove category arguments.

- Current `LogInfo`, `LogWarning`, and `LogError` macros generate log entries and call `util::log::Log(Entry)` even when logging is disabled. `LOG_EMIT` avoids this overhead, which is probably minor but could improve performance in some kernel applications and fuzzing.

- Current `detail_LogWithSrcLoc` macro is dangerous to call because because it does not check for inconsistent or invalid arguments. For example, calling it always bypasses ratelimiting without a check to prevent this. (Previously there was a runtime check, but it was removed without justification in 34332dba2f6f6892859ecb62daa9a2add76ae05e). New `LOG_EMIT` macro is compile-time safe and all the same restrictions as other macros.

- Having multiple implementations of logging macros makes it difficult to add new logging features (see below), because it requires changing many macros and adding separate macro arguments for each feature. Having a single core `LOG_EMIT` macro taking a single compile-time `options` argument makes it possible to add new features cleanly.

Individual commits also implement other improvements: adding missing test coverage and removing misleading `Entry::should_ratelimit` field which is stored in buffered log messages after rate-limiting has been applied, and has no effect.

---

#### Possible followups

This PR does not add any new logging features. It is purely an internal cleanup that fixes the problems listed above. However, it is worth noting that this PR could make it easier to add logging features in the future. For example:

1. New logging options could be added. Examples: `.stacktrace = true` to log the current stack trace, `.exception = true` to log the current exception, `.impossible = true` to indicate an impossible condition and halt fuzzing or request a bug report, `.log_once = true` to log at most once from this source location, `.log_every = 60m` to log at most once per hour, `.dedup = true` to drop duplicste messages, etc.

2. External macros like `LogInfo` and `LogDebug` could accept these options. Example: f5ca95b1e610ebad7063143ddef98fc318251bc4

3. Context information could be added to log messages, e.g., wallet names, chainstate names, or request IDs to distinguish logs from paralell requests. Example: [#30343](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30343)

4. Non-global logging streams could also be supported. For example, kernel functions could accept optional logger arguments instead of always writing to the global logger. Example: [#30342](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30342)

pulls.title: assumeutxo: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.
Require a receiver that has not advanced beyond genesis, already knows the snapshot base header and has no stored blocks beyond genesis or unfinished reindexing.
This removes runtime activation checks, temporary import cache resizing and service demotion while preserving snapshot validation, resumption and background validation.

pulls.title: mempool: recalculate stale BIP68 lockpoints in removeForReorg
pulls.body:
When a reorg lowers the tip, `removeForReorg` can evict BIP68 transactions that are still valid at the new tip, together with all their descendants.

A transaction that spends an unconfirmed parent gets its lockpoints cached with that input at height tip+1. After `invalidateblock`, `TestLockPointValidity` can still pass on those cached lockpoints (always when every input was unconfirmed, since `maxInputBlock` is then genesis; and with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs when the confirmed input's block survives), so `CheckSequenceLocksAtTip` is evaluated against stale values and the transaction is removed.

The fix, suggested by ismaelsadeeq, is to never evict on cached lockpoints alone: if they are not valid at the new tip, or the cached sequence-lock check fails, recalculate them with `CalculateLockPointsAtTip` and evict only if the fresh result also fails. This covers height-based and time-based locks alike, at the cost of some recalculations that turn out to be unnecessary.

test_reorg_stale_lockpoints() in feature_bip68_sequence.py covers four cases across a reorg: a BIP68-disabled child, a BIP68-enabled child of an unconfirmed parent, a child with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs, and a time-based zero lock where the reorg lowers the median time past (test by Bicaru20). The test fails on master, and the mixed-input case also fails on the earlier genesis-only version of this fix.

test_reorg_unsatisfied_lock_evicted() (by instagibbs) is the counterpart: it checks that transactions whose relative lock is genuinely unsatisfied after the reorg are still evicted, together with their descendants.

Reproducer for unpatched nodes:
https://gist.github.com/javierpmateos/c55d365973adbf488a852dc5e0b77dec

Same class of issue fixed for TRUC in #33504.

Closes #35007

net: encapsulate TxRelay state and replace recursive mutexes
pulls.body:
Part of #19303.

This PR refactors per-peer transaction relay state so `TxRelay` owns its guarded data and lock boundaries before replacing its `RecursiveMutex` members with plain `Mutex`.

Before this change, `Peer::TxRelay` was mostly a collection of public state inside `net_processing.cpp`. 
Callers directly locked its mutexes, inspected its fields, and mutated its containers. 
That made the mutex type change hard to review: replacing `RecursiveMutex` with `Mutex` is only clearly safe if outside code cannot accidentally recurse, take locks in the wrong order, or bypass the intended state transitions.

The main changes are:

- Move `Peer::TxRelay` into `node::TxRelay`.
- Route bloom-filter and transaction-inventory state changes through named `TxRelay` methods.
- Remove direct `TxRelay` field and mutex access from `net_processing.cpp`.
- Snapshot queued transaction inventory into a `TxInventoryBatch` in `SendMessages()`, process it without holding the `TxRelay` mutex, and merge unsent entries back afterward.
- Hide the batch backing storage behind a small semantic API.
- Add unit tests and a fuzz target for the extracted `TxRelay` behavior.
- Replace the two `RecursiveMutex` members with `Mutex` and annotate the inventory-before-bloom lock order.

No P2P behavior change is intended. The purpose is to move from "external code locks and mutates TxRelay internals" to "TxRelay owns its state transitions and locking contract."

The most important commit to review is the `SendMessages()` batch snapshot refactor, because that is where the lock ownership model changes. The final mutex replacement is intentionally small after the state has been encapsulated.

pulls.title: coins: tighten cache entry state invariants
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The coins cache still exposed and tested states that production code should not create: standalone `FRESH` entries, non-dirty `BatchWrite()` cursor entries, and spent `FRESH` entries.
That makes the representation harder to reason about, because `CCoinsCacheEntry` stores a separate `DIRTY` bit even though dirty entries are already tracked in the linked list.

**Fix:** This revives and splits the relevant parts of #30673 and #33018.
The series passes freshness through `SetDirty()`, removes fresh-only test states, treats `BatchWrite()` cursor entries as dirty by construction, rejects spent `FRESH` entries, removes the bare `SetFresh()` helper, and derives dirtiness from linked-list membership.
The final commits also tighten `SpendCoin()` around the same cache-state contract: repeated spends of an entry already cached as spent now return false without overwriting caller-owned output, while preserving the already-unchanged cache accounting. Callers must either check the result or explicitly discard it.
`coinscache_sim` now checks the real `SpendCoin()` result against its simulation model, and the no-op repeated-spend path no longer emits the `utxocache:spent` tracepoint because no spend occurs.
Production callers retain their behavior: checked inputs remain spendable, disconnects report unclean state, and replay ignores repeated deletes.

pulls.title: Update libmultiprocess subtree to add nonunix platform support and fix race conditions
pulls.body:
The changes can be verified by running `test/lint/git-subtree-check.sh src/ipc/libmultiprocess` as described in [developer notes](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/developer-notes.md#subtrees) and [lint instructions](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/tree/master/test/lint#git-subtree-checksh).

Changes since last subtree update (#35720):

- Adds support for nonunix platforms, making API changes that are not backwards compatible ([#274](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/274)). Follow-ups add a `CurrentThread()` accessor matching compatibility code in [bitcoin/bitcoin#35084](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35084) ([#323](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/323)) and remove code for Cap'n Proto versions before 0.9 ([#331](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/331)).
- Fixes a data race between IPC calls running on worker threads and disconnects, found by Antithesis ([#349](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/349)).
- Fixes a use-after-free when a socket disconnects before `ConnectStream` connects, and leaks and hangs when a client `construct()` call throws ([#298](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/298)).
- Fixes a race where file descriptors from `SpawnProcess` could leak into processes forked at the same time by other threads, by clearing `FD_CLOEXEC` in the child after forking ([#311](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/311)).
- Makes `SpawnProcess` report `exec` failures back to the parent and throw, reaping the child ([#312](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/312)).
- Adds support for `std::chrono::time_point` fields ([#303](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/303)) and for serializing lists of interface objects that need to be moved from ([#304](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/304)), both needed by [bitcoin/bitcoin#10102](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/10102).
- Accepts container fields and parameters with any comparator, hash, and allocator types, like Bitcoin Core's `GCSFilter::ElementSet`, needed by [bitcoin/bitcoin#29409](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29409) ([#379](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/379)).
- Finds the `capnp` tool in vcpkg and Windows builds, needed by [bitcoin/bitcoin#32387](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32387) ([#317](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/317)).
- Adds a `destroy_connection` option to `ServeStream` and `ConnectStream`, lets `ServeStream` take ownership of the init object and return the new server and its connection, and adds an `EventLoop::incomingConnections()` accessor, simplifying test setup in both repositories and needed by [bitcoin/bitcoin#35932](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35932) ([#365](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/365)).
- Replaces `EventLoop::post()` with `sync()` taking a `kj::FunctionParam`, avoiding a heap allocation per call ([#347](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/347)).
- Names threads spawned by the event loop so they can be told apart in tools and logs ([#324](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/324)).
- Fixes warnings that Bitcoin Core enables or plans to enable: adds `[[noreturn]]` attributes for `-Wmissing-noreturn` ([#339](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/339), for [bitcoin/bitcoin#35911](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35911)), and fixes `-Wunused` ([#362](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/362), for [bitcoin/bitcoin#36167](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36167)), `-Wunused-const-variable` and `-Wundef` ([#370](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/370)), and `-Wmissing-prototypes` ([#386](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/386), for [bitcoin/bitcoin#36743](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36743)) warnings.

pulls.title: validation: improve block data I/O error handling in P2P paths
pulls.body:
Early note: the majority of this PR consists of test coverage. The changes per se are quite small, just the issue shows up in multiple paths in slightly different forms.

The goal of the PR is to ensure I/O errors are not silently ignored during validation or P2P message handling. In some cases, such as `GETDATA` or `GETBLOCKTXN` requests, errors can be swallowed, leaving the node unresponsive to the request without any action. In a harder to reach but more severe case, a swallowed error can leave the node alive but stuck, unable to process new blocks and advance the chain. Also, silently ignoring errors obviously makes problems harder to diagnose. So this PR seeks to improve all of that.

Currently, the same root cause, inability to access the blocks directory, can produce different behaviors depending on where it occurs: 
1. If it happens during block connection, inside `AcceptBlock()`, the error gets caught and triggers a fatal error graceful shutdown. This is the correct behavior.

2. If it happens during block connection (due to the unguarded `FlatFileSeq::Open` -> `fs::create_directories` call), after `AcceptBlock()`, inside `ActivateBestChain()`, the error gets thrown and swallowed by the P2P general try-catch, leaving the node in a living but stuck state. Where `ActivateBestChain()` will always silently fail on any posterior block processing, retrying to active the failing block.

3. If it happens during `GETDATA` request, the file system error gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch, only logging a net-debug-level message. The remote peer is not disconnected, nor the node aborts. It just silently ignores the request. This is different to a missing block data, which currently logs the error + disconnects the peer.

4. If it happens during `GETBLOCKTXN` request, the file system error either gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch or crashes the system via an assertion, depending on if the problem is at the blocks directory level or at the block data level, which is inconsistent.

5. If it happens during `GETCFILTERS` request, the file system error gets swallowed by the message handling general try-catch.

6. If this happens in any of the index functions, the node crashes.


So, this PR makes failure handling consistent and ensures the node never enters a stuck state due to a block I/O error. Changes:

1. `GETDATA` now treats the issue in the same way as other I/O errors: it logs the error + disconnect the remote peer.
2. `GETBLOCKTXN` now triggers a fatal error and graceful shutdown. The error here is stricter than in `GETDATA` because it can only access the last 10 blocks, which must be available for reorgs.
3. `ActivateBestChain()` now triggers a fatal error and graceful shutdown when it happens. Fixing the silent stuck node state scenario.
4. `GETCFILTERS` now logs the error through the expected path: "Failed to find block filter in index". A more descriptive error message can be added in a follow-up PR.
5. The index-related functions now ignore the error instead of crashing the node. This matches how the code was written, as these paths were not expecting `OpenFile` to throw. Better error handling can be added in a follow-up PR.


Testing Note
Can reproduce the different behaviors that cause the stuck node scenario by running the second commit’s unit test 28af683b5dfdce88892e367b308857b94ec630fe or by manually introducing an exception in `ConnectTip()` (which occurs inside `ActivateBestChain()`). Previously, the thrown exception would have being caught by the general P2P try-catch and logged only at net-debug level, which most users do not have enabled, leaving the node alive but stuck, as subsequent block connections repeatedly attempt to process the failing block, throw the exception again, and get silently swallowed. Adding a functional test for this scenario is not possible due to the requirement of failing inside `ActivateBestChain()`, which always occurs after `AcceptBlock()`, which correctly captures the error.


Separate Note
There is another assertion scenario that we can move to graceful shutdown (fatal error) in the compact block relay that I haven't done here.

Extra Note
If want to see a similar error producing a crash, but in the wallet, go to #34176.

pulls.title: coins,dbwrapper: make point-read and txindex lookup failures fatal
pulls.body:
**Problem:** #34931 made unreadable coin entries fatal, but `CDBWrapper::Read()` still returns `false` for deserialization failures and propagates LevelDB point-read exceptions to callers.
A corrupt txindex point read can consequently fail one RPC while the node continues running.
#35728 reports other txindex lookup failures as errors that callers can also catch while the node continues running.
Chainstate also retains `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher` as a separate view layer to report read errors and abort.

**Fix:** Make LevelDB point-read and typed deserialization failures fatal in `CDBWrapper`, after logging the database path and error and notifying the database owner’s `kernel::Notifications` when supplied.
This includes point-read failures during startup, which now bypass the GUI’s database rebuild offer.
Missing keys still return `false`, database-open failures retain their initialization handling, and iterator behavior remains unchanged.

Pass each owner’s existing notifications at construction for chainstate, the block-index database, optional index databases, and the temporary UTXO database used by `dumptxoutset`.
Remove `TryRead()` and `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher`, keep `HaveCoin()` on the cache view that owns its caching behavior, and mark coin-view lookups `noexcept`.

Make txindex consistency errors and block-file lookup failures fatal through the shared notification path before aborting.
Continue skipping stale entries for unknown blocks and non-active blocks without data.
Direct block reads retain their existing RPC error handling.

pulls.title: net: add -outboundbind option for outgoing source address
pulls.body:
Closes #6476

Adds `-outboundbind=<addr>` to set the source address of outgoing clearnet
connections, one per address family. It is separate from `-bind`; without it,
outbound follows the OS routing table as before.

- The command line wins over the config file, as for other options.
- Clearnet only: Tor and I2P use their own transport, CJDNS is direct but not
  IPv4/IPv6, and a proxy leaves the option inert for that family (with a
  startup warning).
- The effective address per family is trial-bound at startup, like `-bind` via
  `BindListenPort`; a port, the wildcard, or a non-clearnet value is rejected. A
  failed bind at connect time aborts the connection, with no fallback.

Functional and unit tests cover both families, the startup rejections, and the
bind-before-connect path.

Based on vasild's approach in
https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/6476#issuecomment-1666472338.

pulls.title: descriptor: speed-up `Parse` (xpub/xpriv) in ~30%
pulls.body:
This PR speeds up descriptor parsing, for basically descriptors that use xpub/xpriv, through some targeted improvements (I've been working on fuzz targets for wallet stuff for a while. I've noticed that some of them are slow so I started to work on understanding why and improve what can be improved. The finding came from it):

- Avoid redundant base58 decoding when parsing extended keys (this is the major improvement)

  ParsePubkeyInner unconditionally called both DecodeExtKey() and DecodeExtPubKey(), each running a full DecodeBase58Check (two SHA256 passes over ~111 bytes). A new DecodeExtKeyOrPubKey() function performs a single base58 decode and then checks the prefix, halving the cryptographic work per key. The interfaces of DecodeSecret, DecodeExtKey, and DecodeExtPubKey are also updated to accept string_view instead of const std::string&, eliminating unnecessary string copies in the descriptor parser and allowing DecodeBase58/DecodeBase58Check to use pointer-range iteration instead of strlen.

- Replace O(n) charset lookup with precomputed table

  DescriptorChecksum previously called std::string::find() for every character in the descriptor string, doing up to 96 comparisons per character. This replaces it with a 256-entry precomputed lookup table for O(1) lookups. The benefit scales with descriptor length.

pulls.title: btcsignals: destroy callbacks on disconnect
pulls.body:
Currently callback functions connected to signals do not get freed when their `connection::disconnect` method is called or when their associated `scoped_connection` is destroyed. They live as long as the signal does, even if they will never be called, and can only get [garbage collected](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/0fd515bbb7070a502dd2fe6d16f5f3cbac591283/src/util/btcsignals.h#L240-L241) if new connections are added.

This behavior is different that previous boost signals behavior and causes a [deadlock](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/31848571315/job/94919834743) on GUI shutdown in #10102 because when the node registers signal callbacks (`handleInitMessage`, etc) that get forwarded to the GUI, the callbacks own `mp::EventLoopRef` references, and if the callbacks aren't freed, the node process can't shut down.

This change restores boost signals behavior freeing callbacks when they are disconnected or when `scoped_connection` objects are destroyed to avoid this problem and make callback lifetimes more predictable.

pulls.title: wallet: rpc: Add snake_case aliases for wallet funding options
pulls.body:
The options for wallet funding RPCs have several issues:

* snake_case aliases are accepted by the server, but unsupported by bitcoin-cli, not mentioned in the docs and rejected by the schema.
* If both the snake_case and camelCase are provided, the camelCase is silently ignored.
* The server silently ignores `subtract_fee_from_outputs`. (reported by stutxo in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35317)

Fix all issues, by:

* Adding the snake_case aliases to the CLI, docs and the schema.
* Rejecting if both are supplied.
* Reading `subtract_fee_from_outputs` instead of silently ignoring it.

pulls.title: crypto: plug hardware optimized SHA256 into libsecp256k1's context
pulls.body:

pulls.title: Reindex: save progress to continue after interruption
pulls.body:
Currently, if the reindex process is interrupted it will start over on next run at `blk00000.dat`. Even after reindexing is finished when the node is in `ActivateBestChain()` an interruption may STILL require a full reindex process because `DB_REINDEX_FLAG` is written `false`, but not flushed.

Mentioned in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/30424 but I couldn't find any specific follow-up:
> There is no reindex progess (it should pick up the previous work and try to make progess)

The solution in this PR is simply to write a new field `DB_REINDEX_LASTFILE` when reindex is interrupted and flush the `DB_REINDEX_FLAG` setting when the process is complete. The complication is that blocks may be out of order on disk and so as we reindex we store orphan blocks temporarily in memory until they are reconnected with their parent in later files. To ensure that data is recovered, the orphan map is serialized and also saved to the database as `DB_REINDEX_ORPHAN_BLOCKS`.

pulls.title: script: clarify implicit signature-cache input requirements
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Signature-cache hashing relies on input requirements that are implicit at its public entry methods.
Inspired by the Elements rangeproof-cache vulnerability behind the recent [Liquid incident](https://blog.blockstream.com/liquid-network-security-incident-assessment) and the [subsequent cache-key fix](https://github.com/ElementsProject/elements/pull/1600), this change clarifies an easy-to-misread hashing pattern: `Write(data, size)` hashes the data bytes without encoding the size.
Bitcoin Core's cache keys already include the signature hash, public key, and signature in separate ECDSA and Schnorr domains.
Bitcoin Core's signature-cache encoding is unambiguous for inputs accepted by its current script checker: a valid ECDSA public key's prefix determines its length, while a Schnorr public key is always 32 bytes, leaving the signature as the remaining suffix.

**Fix:** Use native `HashWriter` serialization in the typed `ComputeEntry*` methods so ECDSA public keys and signature vectors include their CompactSize lengths.
Schnorr retains its fixed-size public-key encoding and raw signature span.
Return the digest by value from the public `ComputeEntry*` methods so callers explicitly initialize the cache entry, where the previous chained `Finalize(entry.begin())` obscured the output assignment.
Keep the prepared salt prefixes private and const, and copy them locally for each entry.
Add a nonce-taking constructor so tests can reproduce the encoding deterministically.
The process-local cache-entry bytes change, while script validity rules are unchanged.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: http: Restore requirement of IPv4 bind success
pulls.body:
### Problem

When bitcoind starts and the HTTP IPv4 listen address is occupied by another process, but the IPv6 address is available, the server fails open and generates a cookie file. When bitcoin-cli runs it picks up the cookie file and sends the credentials in plain text to the non-bitcoind process running on the default IPv4 port. An attacker can then use the credentials to commandeer bitcoind over IPv6.

### Solution

*Safe defaults*:
* When running with default settings, require that the IPv4 bind succeeds.
* When `-rpcbind` is specified, require that all HTTP listen socket binds succeed (fail closed-behavior).

Node runners who only have IPv6 are now required to override `-rpcbind` to only specify the working interface if they were not doing so already.

The problem of bitcoin-cli sending the credentials to what could possibly be the wrong process remains **only in non-default setups**.

### History

40b556d3742a1f65d67e2d4c760d0b13fe8be5b7 from 2015 switched the HTTP server from Boost Asio to LibEvent, and binding switched from an attempt at dual-binding IPv4+v6 and falling back to IPv4-only (rpcserver.cpp / `StartRPCThreads()`), to binding IPv4 *or* IPv6 (httpserver.cpp / `HTTPBindAddresses()`). **The current PR restores the prior behavior of IPv4 being mandatory.**

#14968 from 2018 was an attempt to change the behavior to require *all* binds to succeed. But it ran into issues with poor IPv6 support on CI.

### Severity

This credential exfiltration attack requires capability to launch processes on the bitcoind host. If we are on the same account we can already read the cookie credentials off disk. So it's only really interesting when an attacker is on a different user account on the same host.

### Disclaimer

The 2 commits with multiple authors were probably initially generated with the help of silicon LLMs.

pulls.title: mining: replace interrupt methods with cancellation arguments
pulls.body:
**Depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#342. Only the last commit belongs to this PR.**

---

The blocking methods (`waitTipChanged`, `createNewBlock`, and `BlockTemplate::waitNext`) currently rely on `interrupt()`/`interruptWait()` to cancel them when they are in progress (#33676, #34184). With request cancellation support in libmultiprocess (bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#342), this is no longer needed.

This PR adds `CancelArg` arguments to those blocking methods to register a callback that runs on cancellation and deprecates the interrupt methods. Registering returns a `CancelGuard` that unregisters the callback when destroyed, so the event loop can't run it after the wrapped method goes out of scope.

In the capnp schema, use the `Proxy.extraParam` annotation for the C++ `CancelArg` parameter and the `Cxx.allowCancellation` annotation to enable request cancellation at the RPC layer.

The `CustomBuildExtraParam`/`CustomReadExtraParam` overloads for `CancelArg` live in `ipc/capnp/common-types.h`, following the reference implementation in the libmultiprocess PR. The client side wraps the request in a `kj::Canceler` and throws `InterruptException` when canceled, while the server side registers the method's callback with the request's server context, where the event loop runs it on cancellation.

In tests, update miner_tests to cancel `waitNext()` from another thread, and interface_ipc_mining.py to drop the response promise. Also add `drop_promise()` to ipc_util.py to abandon capnp promises, and a cancelable `waitCancel` method to the ipc_tests `FooInterface` to exercise both the client and server hooks.

Additional note: this is the Bitcoin Core side of approach 4 in #33575.

pulls.title: guix: compute --build triplet when lowering, not at load time
pulls.body:
### Why

`building-on` in `contrib/guix/toolchains.scm` reads `(%current-system)` once, when the module is loaded. `guix shell` loads the manifest before it applies `--system`, so the value is the system of the machine that runs the build, not the system that Guix builds for.

So a build with `ADDITIONAL_GUIX_ENVIRONMENT_FLAGS="--system=aarch64-linux"` on an x86_64 machine (for example with `qemu-binfmt-service-type`, to get an aarch64 build machine) configures the aarch64 cross toolchain with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. `gcc-cross-sans-libc` then fails to configure:

```
checking for CET support... configure: error: compiler and assembler with CET support are required for --enable-cet
```

### What changes

`building-on` becomes a procedure, and its three call sites call it. Guix then computes the triplet for each derivation, under the system that the derivation is built for.

### How I checked

- On master, `HOST=x86_64-linux-gnu guix shell -n --system=aarch64-linux -m contrib/guix/linux_static.scm` (with `toolchains.scm` on the load path, as `guix-build` does) gives `gcc-cross-sans-libc` with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. With this PR it gives `--build=aarch64-guix-linux-gnu`. That is the same derivation that `guix build -d --system=aarch64-linux` gives on master.
- Native builds (no `--system`): the toolchain derivations from `linux_static.scm` and `manifest_gui.scm` are identical on master and with this PR. So this PR does not change release builds.
- With this PR, an emulated aarch64 build of `x86_64-linux-gnu` on x86_64 built the whole cross toolchain and the non-GUI binaries. The GUI environment then failed in the tests of `python-pylint` (timeout under emulation) and `maturin` (snapshot mismatch). These packages have no aarch64 substitutes at the pinned Guix commit, and the failures are not related to this change.

pulls.title: logging: streamline Logger state and drop redundant methods
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The `Logger` class currently tracks enabled log messages using three separate fields:

- `m_categories` — bitmask of enabled log categories
- `m_log_level` — global log level threshold
- `m_category_log_levels` — hash map of per-category level overrides

This representation is confusing and redundant. Bitcoin Core has only ~30 log categories and 2 conditional log levels, so a mutex-protected hash map, a bitset, and a separate global level are unnecessary. The added complexity is also harmful: it makes the code harder to follow, and basic operations like setting a category's level require coordinating multiple fields and method calls.

**Solution:** This PR streamlines the `Logger` class without changing behavior, replacing the three fields with two atomics: one bitmask for each conditional log level (`Debug` and `Trace`). Each bitmask records which categories are enabled at that level.

This allows the following methods to be dropped: `EnableCategory`, `DisableCategory`, `WillLogCategory`, `LogLevel`, `SetLogLevel`, `GetCategoryMask`, `AddCategoryLogLevel`. The remaining `SetCategoryLogLevel` and `WillLogCategoryLevel` methods are now self-contained.

**Behavior note:** This is a behavior-preserving refactor with one exception: categories dynamically enabled at runtime through the `logging` RPC or the kernel `btck_logging_*` API are now always enabled at Debug level, even if `-loglevel=trace` or its kernel equivalent was set at startup. This is unlikely to matter in practice. Very little `LogTrace` logging currently exists, and both APIs are being reworked in bitcoin/bitcoin#34038 and bitcoin/bitcoin#34374. The `-loglevel` option otherwise continues to work as before when categories are not changed at runtime.

pulls.title: Use atomics for determining whether trace logging is enabled
pulls.body:
Followup of #28318, #34038, and #34806 to simplify and optimize the logging-disabled path for `LogTrace()`.

Removes the global log level (`m_log_level`) and the unordered_map from category to level (`m_category_log_levels`) in favour of a single `atomic<uint64_t> m_trace_categories`, and reduces `ShouldDebugLog` and `ShouldTraceLog` to lock-free checks on a single atomic. Also makes `Enabled()` lock-free, to waste a little less time in the case where debugging is completely disabled.

Does a bit of clean up as well:
 * guards `m_file_path` and provides accessors
 * makes other configuration variables atomic, rather than "write-before-createing-threads-then-treat-as-read-only"
 * consolidates duplicated functions (SetCategoryLogLevel, Enable/Trace/DisableCategory, WillLogCategory)

pulls.title: rpc: add key-origin modes to PSBT processing RPCs
pulls.body:
This PR extends the existing `bip32derivs` argument of the
`walletprocesspsbt` and `descriptorprocesspsbt` RPCs with explicit key-origin
modes.

## Motivation

Setting `bip32derivs=false` prevents new key-origin fields from being added, but
does not explicitly remove fields already present in an input PSBT. Some
collaborative PSBT workflows need to remove that metadata before sharing the
PSBT.

## Behavior

- `true` or `"add"` allows known key-origin fields to be added.
- `false` or `"preserve"` does not add or explicitly remove key-origin fields.
- `"strip"` does not add key-origin fields and removes surviving standard
  key-origin fields after normal processing.

The default remains `true`. The existing boolean values remain accepted for
compatibility.

Stripping removes global xpubs and legacy and Taproot BIP32 derivation fields
from inputs and outputs. Unknown and proprietary PSBT fields are left
unchanged. Finalization may independently remove input key-origin fields.

Closes #30294.

pulls.title: bip352: skip scriptSig eval for non-segwit P2SH inputs
pulls.body: Only P2SH-P2WPKH inputs are eligible, which require a non-empty witness. Consensus forbids a witness on non-segwit P2SH inputs, so check the witness (and the cheap pubkey size check) before evaluating the scriptSig. This avoids evaluating scriptSigs of up to `MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE` for the common case of non-segwit P2SH spends.

pulls.title: logging: make trace logging easily usable
pulls.body:
**Problem**: Currently it is difficult to enable `trace` logging. 

The `-loglevel=trace` setting works, but does nothing by default and needs to be combined with `-debug` settings to have an effect.

Additionally, it is not possible to switch between `debug` and `trace` logging at runtime without restarting the node. These problems make `trace` logging less useful than it could be, effectively make existing `trace` logs undiscoverable, and making it not worthwhile to add new tracing.

**Solution**: Fix these issues by allowing the `-loglevel` option to work without an accompanying `-debug` option, and by adding a matching `loglevel` RPC that allows log levels to be configured at runtime.

**Usage examples**:
```bash
bitcoin rpc loglevel                               # See current log levels
bitcoin rpc loglevel trace                         # Set global level to -loglevel=trace
bitcoin rpc loglevel debug                         # Set global level to -loglevel=debug
bitcoin rpc loglevel info                          # Set global level to -loglevel=info
bitcoin rpc loglevel libevent=info                 # Set category level to -loglevel=libevent:info
bitcoin rpc loglevel trace net=debug libevent=info # Set global & category levels to -loglevel=trace,net:debug,libevent:info
```

**Compatibility:** This PR is backwards compatible and doesn't change the `-debug` and `-debugexclude` options (which become synonyms for `-loglevel=debug` and `-loglevel=info`, respectively). The `logging` RPC is also mostly unchanged, except now it validates category names before updating log levels, instead of failing with half-applied changes. Also the `logging` RPC now only toggles between `info` and `debug` levels instead of trying to remember previously assigned levels, which was needlessly confusing.

pulls.title: test: make p2p_eviction actually exercise block-time protection
pulls.body:
`p2p_eviction.py` tests that 4 inbound peers that recently sent us a novel block are protected from eviction. However, the test currently passes even when that protection is not in effect. 

The block-sending peers are connected first, so they are the oldest connections. When block-time protection doesn't apply, `CompareNodeBlockTime` falls back to connection time and protects the 4 oldest peers, which are these same peers. Then the youngest remaining peer gets evicted. The check `evicted_peers[0] not in protected_peers` therefore holds whether or not block-time protection works.

This can be shown by deleting the line where the peers send their block (L71 on master):
```py
block_peer.send_blocks_and_test([block], node, success=True)
```

pulls.title: wallet: fail dump on incomplete writes
pulls.body:
This makes `bitcoin-wallet dump` fail if writing the dump file does not complete successfully.

Previously, `DumpWallet()` only checked whether the dump file could be opened. If later writes or close failed, the tool could still return success and print the private-key warning, leaving a truncated dump file behind.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. Small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: RFC: consensus: Make `CAmount` a class
pulls.body:
We should treat people's money with care across node and wallet.

Having our `CAmount` be a `typedef` for raw `int64_t` as on master has the following drawbacks:
* Allows assigning to from `bool`s, leading to the issues like the one previously fixed by 0026b330c4abbbbdb96e4f0c4d380d70d8e592ab.
* Allows direct comparison with integral types of differing size, leading to things like the issue previously fixed by 890a09b1e49925315a5636f29cc5af36928fe092 (reverting it on top of this PR leads to compile errors).
* Allows forgetting to initialize amounts (`CAmount fee;`).
* Allows direct operations with imprecise decimal types as in `CAmount target = 49.5L * COIN` in src/wallet/test/coinselector_tests.cpp.
* Allows *multiplying* two `CAmount`s with each other, which does not make sense.

Beyond fixing the above, this PR also makes amounts stick out more in code - either by the `CAmount` type itself or by using the `sats` unit specifier.

This work is also a stepping stone for possible future work introducing an even safer amount type which only allows values in the range `[0, MAX_MONEY]`.

Already merged PRs spawned out of this work: #35456, #35372

Prior attempts in similar directions: #5430, #4067

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

Later commits also introduce stricter checking during deserialization, rejecting the following before fully deserializing:
* Transactions with more inputs/outputs than are possible in a valid transaction.
* Transactions with 0 inputs or 0 outputs (applied in P2P, but not RPC etc. for backward compatibility).
* Transactions/blocks that exceed the 4M weight limit (also only applied in P2P).

The result is a significant reduction in the worst-case time and memory allocations needed for deserialization, both in valid and invalid transactions. With it, the worst-case memory of a valid deserialized block drops from 106.8 MiB to 6.0 MiB. Memory usage during deserialization can temporarily be higher: up to 7.8 MiB for valid blocks, and up to 13.4 MiB for invalid blocks, which can combine a few temporary vector allocations of up to 5 MB each.

Deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR. Runtimes are medians in milliseconds. Memory usage is in MiB, and ✕ means rejected at deserialization time. Peak memory refers to the memory during deserialization itself, not persisted in the deserialized `CBlock` object. Numbers over 50 ms, 20 MiB usage, or 100 MiB peak are in **bold**.

| block | gcc | clang | mem | peak mem |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Valid blocks** |
| 1 tx, max 1-byte wit elems | **99.1** → 16.0 | **111.4** → 21.9 | **106.8** → 3.8 | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, max empty wit elems | **279.2** → 18.7 | **293.7** → 25.1 | **91.5** → 3.8 | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout, 1-item wit | 12.33 → 13.39 | 15.00 → 15.43 | 6.7 → 6.0 | 6.7 → 6.0 |
| max txs, 1 txin and 1 txout | 6.43 → 7.04 | 7.87 → 8.30 | 5.8 → 5.6 | 5.8 → 5.6 |
| 1 tx, max txins, 1-elem wit | 4.53 → 4.68 | 5.04 → 5.37 | 4.0 → 2.9 | 4.0 → 2.9 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 5.30 → 5.47 | 5.97 → 6.20 | 3.5 → 2.9 | 3.5 → 2.9 |
| **Invalid blocks** |
| 400k txs, many wit elems, truncated | **84.8** → 16.1 | **95.6** → 21.8 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 12.6 |
| 400k txs, big wit+scriptsig, truncated | **84.0** → 16.1 | **96.0** → 21.7 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 13.4 |
| 1 tx, 2M 1-byte wit elems | **98.0** → 10.6 | **109.9** → 16.2 | **106.8** → ✕ | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, 4M empty wit elems | **271.0** → 13.4 | **288.9** → 19.6 | **91.6** → ✕ | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max empty txs | **101.0** → 0.006 | **139.0** → 0.008 | **67.1** → ✕ | 67.1 → 4.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout | 27.6 → 7.3 | 34.5 → 8.5 | **23.4** → ✕ | 23.4 → 6.4 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

Some notable changes:
* By implementing some checks (for inherently consensus-invalid things) in the deserialization logic, behavior may change. In particular, deserialization errors in P2P cause messages to be dropped/ignored, rather than triggering validation or net processing logic (which may include disconnections and/or inserting into reject filters).
* The rejection of transactions with too many inputs or outputs applies everywhere, including in RPC. That's hopefully a desirable change, but a change in behavior still.
* Random access to the witness stack elements becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This is not a problem for any validation logic, but may be relevant for the libbitcoinkernel API which exposes an individual element accessor.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

There are a few possible follow-ups:
* Enforce the 400k WU policy limit during transaction deserialization when active (instead of the 4M WU consensus limit).
* Extend this approach to entire `CTransaction`, allowing all transaction data to be stored packed together in a few allocations (rather than one per input, one per output, one per witness) plus some index structure to access it efficiently. That's a much bigger change, needing abstractions like #35569, but would reduce the maximum memory usage per WU for valid blocks from around 1.5 bytes/WU to 1.1 bytes/WU (compared to ~28 bytes/WU in master).

pulls.title: kernel, validation: Add btck_chainstate_manager_set_clock_time
pulls.body:
The main commit in this PR is the second commit adding a `btck_chainstate_manager_set_clock_time` API which lets kernel applications run validation code deterministically without depending on the system clock. This is an alternative to #35496, and one of several alternatives discussed in that PR, with some tradeoffs described in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35496#issuecomment-4735710317. The other commits are indirectly related and could be moved to separate PRs (or dropped):
Details

- The first commit fixes a timing race in the `chainstatemanager_ibd_exit_after_loading_blocks` test that happened because test code and validation code (in `UpdateIBDStatus`) were both calling `NodeClock::now()` to get the current clock time, and test relied on the times being the same for `tip_recent=true` checks. The failure this fixes should be rare, but I noticed it when I experimented with making time comparison in `IsTipRecent` more precise. - The third commit refactors mempool code to use a consistent way of getting and representing clock times, allowing the fourth commit to enforce that no libbitcoinkernel code uses nondeterministic clock times unintentionally. The third and fourth commits do not need to be part of this PR, but I implemented them to be sure the main commit was complete and all call sites were using the right clock times.

pulls.title: wallet: harden the read-only BDB parser against crafted files
pulls.body:
The read-only BDB parser in migrate.cpp runs on any file passed to `migratewallet`
(RPC or GUI) or `bitcoin-wallet`. #34959 added checks for btree levels and overflow
lengths, which stop simple cycles, but a crafted file can still make the parser hang
or use a lot of memory:

- A btree page can be the child of more than one internal page. Its level still
  checks out, so it gets parsed again for every path that reaches it. On master an
  ~8 KB file built this way doesn't finish.
- An overflow page with no data doesn't count toward the length #34959 checks, so
  two such pages pointing at each other loop forever. Separately, any number of
  records can point at the same overflow chain, and each one reads and stores its
  own copy.
- All of a page's index entries can point at the same record, which then gets read
  and kept once per entry. A single 64 KB page can turn into ~500 MB this way. On
  master a 256 KB file took `migratewallet` from 54 MB to ~800 MB.

The first two are fixed by tracking visited pages (the approach from #34946): btree
pages in one set, and overflow pages in another that covers the whole tree. For the
third, a page is rejected once its records add up to more than the page size.

This shouldn't affect real wallets. In a valid btree every page has a single parent
and every overflow page belongs to a single record. Records on a page can't overlap
either, since the parser already rejects databases that allow duplicates.

Each fix comes with a test in db_tests.cpp that builds the bad file by hand, plus a
test that a page filled to the last byte still parses. `wallet_migration.py` passes
with v28.2.

The last commit adds two errors from #34959 to the `wallet_bdb_parser` fuzz target.
They were missing, so the target aborted on inputs that reach them. I ran into this
while feeding mutated copies of the test files through the target.

Supersedes #35992.

pulls.title: refactor: Change some validation.cpp methods to return BlockValidationState
pulls.body:
**Summary**. Refactor validation result to be a return value instead of an output parameter in several `validation.cpp` methods.

**Motivation**. The benefits of the change are:
- Exclude the potentially inconsistent case when the bool return value and the returned `state` are inconsistent
- Exclude the ambiguity whether the passed in value of state is used or not (not obvious in chained calls)
- Remove the possibility of unintuitive interaction between subsequent calls with the same state. In case of a validation error, a failure reason is set if the state was valid, but not if it was already invalid.
- Slightly simpler: It's more evident which is the result; one less parameters.

This has grown out from #33856, mentioned in [comment here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#pullrequestreview-4276791829) and [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#issuecomment-4477751949).

**Details**. Many methods follow the scheme where the validation state is returned in an output parameter (`BlockValidationState& state`), and and additional `bool` return value indicating success. In success case the convention is that `state.IsValid()` and the return value are both true. After the change there is only a `BlockValidationState` return value, which is either success (`state.IsValid() == true`), or an invalid/error case.

This change is a highly localized refactor, but touching a sensitive file.

Relevant methods called by `ProcessNewBlockHeaders` and `AcceptBlock` (directly and indirectly) are touched.

Changes are separated into commits by touched methods, ordered by bottom-to-top in the call hierarchy.

pulls.title: RFC: Separate out runtime errors from BlockValidationState using `util::Expected`
pulls.body:
`BlockValidationState` currently carries two unrelated kinds of failure: consensus/policy invalidity which is the actual purpose and runtime errors via a `M_ERROR` mode in `ModeState` enum inside `ValidationState` class. This PR removes `M_ERROR` and routes runtime errors through `util::Expected<T, std::string>` instead, making the two failure modes distinct.

## Motivation

`BlockValidationState` exists to describe why a block or transaction is invalid. It holds a consensus/policy reject reason. A disk write or system runtime error is not that, yet it was folded into the same object as a third state i.e. `M_ERROR`.

This conflation has two costs:

- Wrong abstraction for non-validating functions. `FlushStateToDisk`, `DisconnectTip`, `ActivateBestChain`, `PreciousBlock`, and `InvalidateBlock` do no block validation, but each takes a `BlockValidationState` out-param to report any runtime error.

- Three outcomes in one object. Functions that can both validate and hit a runtime error (`ConnectBlock`, `AcceptBlock`, `ProcessNewBlock`) holds valid, invalid, and fatal into a single `BlockValidationState`, forcing every caller to unwrap.

As noted in the original discussion [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#discussion_r2765218331):

> Functions like FlushStateToDisk, ActivateBestChain aren't exactly about validating a certain block, yet they take a BlockValidationState& out-param just to absorb runtime errors, which feels like the wrong abstraction.

And also discussion [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-4783419874) to remove `M_ERROR` value.

- This would also pave a long term fix for #35570, which returns `BlockValidationState` from validation methods instead of boolean value.

`util::Expected` is a good option for this reason, it keeps the error handling in the same return value style (system/runtime errors and `ValidationState` for consensus correctness) and separates-out runtime errors from `ValidationState`.


Runtime errors could be signaled either by a return value or by throwing. This PR keeps them as return values as it's a minimal  change. `M_ERROR` was already a return-value mechanism  included in `ValidationState` with consensus verdict. This PR doesn't open the exceptions vs returns question, it keeps the existing return-value style and just moves the fatal error into a proper Expected channel.
