pulls.title: qa: assert_equals -> assert_true/assert_false
pulls.body:
Instead of this in the functional tests:
```python
    assert_equals([long expression pushing next arg to the right], True)
    assert_equals([other long expression pushing next arg to the right], False)
```
we get:
```python
    assert_true([long expression without arg on the right side..])
    assert_false([other long expression without next arg to the right.])
```

The main point of this change is that `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` reduce cognitive tokens when scanning the code (equals to *what*...?). (As a consequence, `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` are also common in other test frameworks).

`assert_equals()` continues to be used in cases where we don't compare to boolean literals.

`assert_true([expression])` is different from plain `assert [expression]` in that `assert` is truthy while `assert_true` requires boolean `True`. (`assert` can also be deactivated when executing Python code in optimized mode (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30529#discussion_r1893029530)).

A smaller scale attempt at introducing `assert_true()` was originally included in #31874 before being dropped.

pulls.title: descriptor: Represent multipath descriptors in a single Descriptor object
pulls.body:
Currently, multipath descriptor strings treat the multipath specifiers as syntactic sugar. Once we finish parsing such a string, the multipath elements are lost as the result is the multiple distinct descriptors that the multipath is a shorthand for. This means that we are unable to return the multipath string for such descriptors.

This PR allows descriptors to actually be multipath where the multipath specifiers are represented inside of the paths of `BIP32PubkeyProvider`s. This allows for the multipath string to be produced.

In order to achieve this, a lot of derivation path parsing is refactored. `KeyPath` is promoted to being its own class (which subclasses `std::vector`), while the individual derivation indexes become a `KeyPathElement` object so that the multipath elements can be represented. Furthermore, hardened derivation characters are now being stored within `KeyPathElement`s so each element knows what the original hardened character was. This also cleans up a little bit of the descriptor implementation as we no longer have to carry around `bool apostrophe` in a bunch of places.

Lastly, `Parse` now returns a single `Descriptor` object, rather than a vector of them. If the descriptor is a multipath descriptor, the expansion can be retrieved using `GetMultipathExpansion()`. The wallet uses this and still must not store multipath descriptors.

pulls.title: descriptor: Reconstruct a multipath descriptor from its expansion
pulls.body:
#36442 allows multipath descriptors to be represented in a single `Descriptor` object. `GetMultipathExpansion` returns the multiple descriptors represented by a multipath descriptor. This expansion is reversible - given the expansion in the order of the multipath elements, it is possible to determine what the original multipath descriptor was. This PR adds `ReconstructMultipath` to produce a new `Descriptor` representing the multipath descriptor that produced the expansion.

Depends on #36442

pulls.title: wallet: Store information about created and imported multipath descriptors
pulls.body:
The wallet does not store any information about multipath descriptors. When a multipath descriptor is imported, it is first expanded, then the expansion descriptors are imported into the wallet.

This PR adds a field to `WalletDescriptor` which stores the IDs of the ScriptPubKeyMans of the descriptors that are part of the expansion, in the order that they are expanded. This allows us to use `ReconstructMultipath` to produce the multipath descriptor when necessary.

This is useful for working with hardware wallets that require policy registration, particularly those that require resending the descriptor that was registered.

`listdescriptors` is updated to include a `multipath_descriptor` field which contains the multipath descriptor for each individual descriptor if it originally came from a multipath descriptor.

Lastly, the automatically generated descriptors are now produced and stored as multipath descriptors, so `listdescriptors` will provide a `multipath_descriptor` for everything that the wallet automatically generates.

Note that the IDs stored in the wallet are ScriptPubKeyMan IDs, which we cannot compute from a descriptor as we assume to be opaque blobs since #35445.

Alternative to #36133, depends on #36442 and #36443

pulls.title: torcontrol: send -torpassword hex-encoded to avoid escaping bugs
pulls.body:
The Tor password was sent as a `QuotedString` with only double quotes escaped; as Tor interprets backslash escapes inside it, any password containing a backslash was mangled (or left the string unterminated).

The Tor Control spec deliberately allows the token to be sent as unquoted hex "to avoid escaping issues", as the `SAFECOOKIE` response already is. This patch does the same for the password, and also adds a functional test covering backslashes and quotes.

pulls.title: kernel: Add script evaluation tracer
pulls.body:
This adds a callback hook to the kernel library C header for getting the current script evaluation state on each script evaluation step. This can be used for debugging scripts and gives external applications a view into how Bitcoin Core does script evaluation.

The initial sketch for this work was prepared on rust-bitcoinkernel: https://github.com/sedited/rust-bitcoinkernel/tree/feature_script_debug . That branch also includes a very rudimentary script debugger showcasing the use case for this patch. Clankers seems to do a decent job at coding up prototypes for more featureful debuggers, which seems like a fun project to hack on if anybody else wants to give it a try.

This feature is gated behind the ENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE flag. To compile with the feature enabled, pass `-DENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE=ON`. If the feature is not manually enabled, the trace hooks are stubbed out.

The traces are divided into separate frames. RAII is used to guarantee that every script evaluation has at least its start and end state captured. Each instruction generates a unique frame as well.

The ScriptError in the VerifyScript invocation run when calling script_pubkey_verify is added in order to be able to surface the error code in the trace frames.

Another use case could also be using the frames to ensure that the script interpreter is actually doing what we think it is doing during the script tests. This might prevent unit test bugs in the future, i.e. when [error conditions shadow actual behaviour](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33961), and could also be interesting for fuzzing the script interpreter.

pulls.title: mining: add TxCollection to bandwidth-efficiently validate external block templates
pulls.body:
The Stratum v2 spec defines a [Job Declarator Server](https://stratumprotocol.org/specification/06-job-declaration-protocol) (JDS), whose job it is to approve custom miner templates. Since #34020 it can use `getTransactionsByWitnessID()` to request transactions from the node, instead of maintaining its own mempool mirror (see https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/pull/911), and then request any missing transactions from the miner.

The new `TxCollection` interface introduced by this PR optimizes this further. We build and validate the block template ourselves now, based on the requested transaction list and our own mempool, so known transactions don't need to cross the IPC boundary. This also fits the [draft spec](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-spec/discussions/239) for JDS custom job validation through a Template Provider.

The following flow is demonstrated in https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/pull/599:

1. Miner generates a template, e.g. using our `createNewBlock()` IPC method
2. They send the list of `Wtxid`s to the pool's JDS
3. JDS calls `Mining::collectTxs()` (this PR) with that `Wtxid` list
4. We check the list against our mempool and hold a `CTransactionRef` for each match
5. The JDS queries `unknownTxPos()` to learn what's missing from the collection
6. The JDS requests the fully serialized missing transactions from the miner (using native Stratum v2 messages)
7. JDS calls `addMissingTxs()` which completes the collection
8. JDS calls `makeTemplate()` which reconstructs the block and validates it, optionally with the coinbase it intends to use (e.g. to check the reward amount); a node-generated dummy is used otherwise. The JDS needs the check to succeed, may relay the BIP-22 failure reason to the miner.
9. It returns a `BlockTemplate` which works as if we generated the template ourselves, but with methods like `waitNext()` disabled. The JDS can call `submitSolution()` (the sv2 spec allows for redundant block reconstruction by both the miner node and the JDS).

If this sounds very similar to compact block relay: it is! In fact, it would be easy to expand the above methods to take transaction short ids instead of `Wtxid`. That may be useful for the [p2pool revival project](https://www.vinteum.org/blog/reviving-p2pool-welcoming-johnny-santos-as-a-vinteum-grantee), which needs a way to validate and relay weak blocks as compact blocks. The p2pool client software would need to (trivially) verify the PoW, but could use the `TxCollection` interface to reconstruct and verify the block content. That said, the SRI [JDS](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20JDS) implementation is much further along and likely to be the first consumer of this.

Commits:

- _ipc: add TxCollection scaffold_ - step 3 and 4
- _mining: add TxCollection unknownTxPos_ - step 5
- _mining: add TxCollection addMissingTxs_ - step 7
- _mining: add coinbase transaction helper_ - we need a dummy coinbase to verify the block, so extract a helper from `BlockAssembler::CreateNewBlock()`
- _mining: assemble block templates from TxCollection_ - step 8, node implementation
- _ipc: expose TxCollection template creation_ - step 8 and 9, including restrictions on externally generated templates
- _mining: allow TxCollection templates to use a supplied coinbase_ - optional coinbase in step 8

Potential followups:

- https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/122
- expose total fees for externally generated templates, building on #36525
- have `addMissingTxs()` (optionally) insert favorable transactions into our mempool
- add a data structure to store transactions that don't meet our mempool threshold (so `TxCollection` can grab them, instead of needing another round trip)

pulls.title: [DONTMERGE] Test run with reproducer for forced chunked recv
pulls.body:
WARNING: NOT INTENDED FOR MERGING!

Performing a test run with forced chunked recv. 

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure.

This branch contains a stress test reproducer. For every socket read, `recv()` is not called to read all available data, but data is read and returned in smaller chunks. The goal is to test code for robustness in face of unexpected chunking of the data.

This PR will be closed once the test runs complete, and kept for reference (some tests are expected to fail).

Similar to #36724 .

pulls.title: lint: have git-subtree-check check for backportability
pulls.body:
A subtree update is easier to backport when its merge commit is based on the previous subtree merge instead of on a newer `master` commit. The exact same merge commit can then be reused on release branches, making the backport trivial to verify without rereviewing a newly generated subtree merge.

Update `git-subtree-check.sh` to locate the merge that introduced the latest subtree squash reachable from `COMMIT` and error if its first parent is not the previous subtree merge.

Sometimes subtree and Bitcoin Core API changes are incompatible, making it necessary to base an update on a later commit. Add `--incompatible` to explicitly skip the backportability check in that case.

The CI lint job always sets `--incompatible`, so we rely on reviewers to run the new check.

As a preparatory refactor, replace `getopts` with explicit option parsing and add `--remote` as the preferred long alias for `-r`.

Example that passes:

```sh
test/lint/git-subtree-check.sh src/ipc/libmultiprocess 66b4e30e
```

Example that errors because the update is not based on the previous subtree merge:

```sh
test/lint/git-subtree-check.sh src/ipc/libmultiprocess 02afa661
```

pulls.title: test: look for the wtxid in p2p_blocksonly
pulls.body:
In `blocks_relay_conn_tests`, the check that a transaction submitted over RPC is not announced to a block-relay-only peer looks for its txid among the peer's invs. The peer is a `P2PTxInvStore`, which negotiates wtxidrelay, so an announcement would carry the wtxid. The MiniWallet transaction has a witness, so its txid and wtxid differ, and the check passes whether or not the node announces it.

This checks the wtxid instead. To see the difference, open that connection as `outbound-full-relay`: the old check still passes, the new one fails. It also adds an `outbound-full-relay` peer that must receive the wtxid announcement first, so the check cannot pass silently again.

#35920 also edits `blocks_relay_conn_tests`; the two do not conflict.

Found while porting these tests to https://github.com/btclib-org/bitcoin-node-tests.

pulls.title: torcontrol: escape backslashes in -torpassword
pulls.body:
With `HASHEDPASSWORD` authentication, `TorController::protocolinfo_cb` sends the password as a quoted string, `AUTHENTICATE "<password>"` (torcontrol.cpp:667). It escapes `"` but not `\`.

Tor parses that argument as a control-spec QuotedString, where a backslash escapes the next character. So:

- `-torpassword=pa\ss` reaches Tor as `pass`, authentication fails and no onion service is created
- `-torpassword=pass\` escapes the closing quote, so the command is malformed

This escapes backslashes before quotes.

The new `test_password_escaping` in `feature_torcontrol.py` uses the mock control server with `HASHEDPASSWORD` and `-torpassword=pa\ss"word\`, and checks the exact `AUTHENTICATE` line. On master it gets `AUTHENTICATE "pa\ss\"word\"`, with the fix `AUTHENTICATE "pa\\ss\"word\\"`.

Tested against Tor 0.4.9.12 with `HashedControlPassword` set for `pa\ss"word\`: on master bitcoind logs "tor: Authentication failed", with this change authentication succeeds and ADD_ONION creates the onion service.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.
